resources.string: Simplified oblique view of the right knee. The kneecap and front of the joint capsule are omitted so the two bands are visible. The arrows show directions of sliding that the ligaments resist, not how far the bones move or how much force the bands carry.
Ligaments are collagen-rich bands that help stabilize joints. Unlike muscles, they do not contract to move the bones. They resist certain motions as their fibers come under tension.
Two bands cross inside the knee

The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) runs from the inner face of the lateral femoral condyle to the front of the area between the tibial condyles. The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) runs from the inner face of the medial femoral condyle to the back of that area, down the rear slope of the tibia.
The ACL helps limit how far the tibia slides forward relative to the femur. The band stays attached at both ends and resists the slide in tension.
The PCL helps limit how far the tibia slides backward relative to the femur. Its different attachment sites let it resist sliding in the opposite direction.
The two bands guide without locking

The knee still bends and straightens. As posture and load change, different fibers can carry more or less tension. The cruciates work with the shapes of the bones and the other tissues around the knee; they do not hold the joint rigid.
